Enhancing molecular property prediction with quantized GNN models


[Download PDF](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3.pdf)

## Abstract

Efficient and reliable prediction of molecular properties, such as water solubility, hydration free energy, lipophilicity, and quantum mechanical properties, is essential for rational compound design in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have significantly advanced molecular property prediction tasks, their high memory footprint, computational demands, and inference latency are often overlooked. These challenges hinder the deployment of property prediction models on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT devices. Therefore, optimizing storage, reducing resource consumption, and improving inference speed are crucial. This paper presents a systematic approach to molecular networks by integrating GNN models with the DoReFa-Net quantization algorithm. The proposed method aims to enhance computational efficiency while maintaining predictive performance, enabling lightweight yet effective models suitable for molecular task. The study investigates the impact of different bitwidth quantization levels on model performance, using metrics such as RMSE and MAE. Results show that, for physical chemistry datasets, the effectiveness of quantization is highly dependent on the model architecture. Notably, the quantum mechanical dipole moment task maintains strong performance up to 8-bit precision, achieving similar or slightly better results. However, extreme quantization, particularly at 2-bit precision, severely degrades performance, highlighting the limitations of aggressive compression.

## Introduction

Cheminformatics, the field dedicated to applying computational methods for analyzing chemical data, has witnessed extensive research on artificial intelligence approaches, particularly machine learning, for several decades \[ [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR1 "Varnek A, Baskin I (2012) Machine learning methods for property prediction in chemoinformatics: Quo Vadis? J Chem Inf Model 52(6):1413–1437"), [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR2 "Mitchell JB (2014) Machine learning methods in chemoinformatics. Wiley Interdis Cip Rev Comput Mol Sci 4(5):468–481"), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR3 "Chen G, Shen Z, Iyer A, Ghumman UF, Tang S, Bi J, Li Y (2020) Machine learning-assisted de novo design of organic molecules and polymers: opportunities and challenges. Polymers 12(1):163")\]. Machine learning in chemistry utilizes a diverse toolkit, combining well-established models with advanced deep learning \[ [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR4 "Goodfellow I, Bengio Y, Courville A (2016) Deep learning. MIT press, Cambridge")\] techniques inspired by breakthroughs in computer vision (e.g., convolutional neural networks \[ [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR5 "LeCun Y, Kavukcuoglu K, Farabet C (2010). Convolutional networks and appli cations in vision. In Proceedings of 2010 IEEE international symposium on circuits and systems. IEEE: New York. Pp. 253–256. ")\]) and natural language processing (e.g., sequence models \[ [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR6 "Schwaller P, Laino T, Gaudin T, Bolgar P, Hunter CA, Bekas C, Lee AA (2019) Molecular transformer: a model for uncertainty-calibrated chemical reaction prediction. ACS Cent Sci 5(9):1572–1583")\]). Deep learning methods have become increasingly popular across various research domains \[ [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR7 "Ul Rahman J, Danish S, Lu D (2023) Deep neural network-based simulation of Sel’kov model in glycolysis: a comprehensive analysis. Mathematics 11(14):3216"), [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR8 "Ul Rahman J, Chen Q, Yang Z (2020) Additive parameters for deep face recognition. Commun Math Stat 8:203–217"), [9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR9 "Rahman JU, Danish S, Lu D (2024) Oscillator simulation with deep neural networks. Mathematics 12(7):959"), [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR10 "Rahman JU, Makhdoom F, Lu D. (2023) Amplifying sine unit: an Oscilla tory activation function for deep neural networks to recover nonlinear oscillations efficiently. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:2304.09759                                    .")\], particularly in drug discovery, where they address critical tasks such as molecular property prediction \[ [11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR11 "Xu L, Pan S, Xia L, Li Z (2023) Molecular property prediction by combining LSTM and GAT. Biomolecules 13(3):503")\], drug-target affinity prediction \[ [12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR12 "Xia L, Xu L, Pan S, Niu D, Zhang B, Li Z (2023) Drug-target binding affinity prediction using message passing neural network and self supervised learning. BMC Genom 24(1):557"), [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR13 "Pan S, Xia L, Xu L, Li Z (2023) SubMDTA: drug target affinity prediction based on substructure extraction and multi-scale features. BMC Bioinform 24(1):334")\], and protein–protein interaction prediction \[ [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR14 "Li X, Han P, Wang G, Chen W, Wang S, Song T (2022) SDNN-PPI: self attention with deep neural network effect on protein-protein interaction prediction. BMC Genom 23(1):474")\]. These approaches have significantly improved the analysis and prediction of chemical compound properties, accelerating the drug development process.

Molecular property prediction serves as a cornerstone of drug design, aiming to identify molecules with desired attributes such as solubility, stability, or biological activity from extensive molecular datasets. Central to the success of these predictive tasks is the use of effective molecular representations, which have emerged as a crucial factor in advancing drug discovery and materials science \[ [15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR15 "Shen J, Nicolaou CA (2019) Molecular property prediction: recent trends in the era of artificial intelligence. Drug Discov Today Technol 32:29–36"), [16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR16 "Pollice R, dos Passos Gomes G, Aldeghi M, Hickman RJ, Krenn M, Lavigne C, Aspuru-Guzik A (2021) Data-driven strategies for accelerated materials design. Acc Chem Res 54(4):849–860"), [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR17 "Xiong Z, Wang D, Liu X, Zhong F, Wan X, Li X, Zheng M (2019) Pushing the boundaries of molecular representation for drug discovery with the graph attention mechanism. J Med Chem 63(16):8749–8760"), [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR18 "Walters WP, Barzilay R (2020) Applications of deep learning in molecule gener ation and molecular property prediction. Acc Chem Res 54(2):263–270"), [19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR19 "Yang K, Swanson K, Jin W, Coley C, Eiden P, Gao H, Barzilay R (2019) Analyzing learned molecular representations for property prediction. J Chem Inf Model 59(8):3370–3388")\]. Historically, molecular descriptors like molecular fingerprints \[ [20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR20 "Rogers D, Hahn M (2010) Extended-connectivity fingerprints. J Chem Inf Model 50(5):742–754")\] and Coulomb matrices \[ [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR21 "Rupp M, Tkatchenko A, Muller KR, Von Lilienfeld OA (2012) Fast and accurate modeling of molecular atomization energies with machine learning. Phys Rev Lett 108(5):058301")\] were manually engineered or computed and used as inputs for machine learning algorithms, including random forests \[ [22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR22 "Breiman L (2001) Random forests. Mach Learn 45:5–32")\] and support vector machines \[ [23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR23 "Cortes C (1995) Support-vector networks. Mach Learn 20:273–297")\]. However, these hand-crafted features often fell short in representing the full complexity of molecular systems, as they were not optimized for specific predictive objectives and could sometimes include redundant or irrelevant information.

To address these limitations, researchers have embraced a more intuitive molecular representation by modeling molecules as graphs, where atoms are represented as nodes and chemical bonds or spatial proximities are modeled as edges. In this graph-based framework, molecular property prediction tasks leverage graph representation learning to capture the intricate relationships within molecules. Among these advancements, GNNs have emerged as powerful tools for modeling such data. These networks utilize a “message-passing” mechanism to update node embeddings based on surrounding graph structures. Kipf and Welling introduced the Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), which applied spectral graph convolutions to effectively learn node representations, achieving state-of-the-art results in various graph-based tasks \[ [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR24 "Kipf TN, Welling, M. (2016) Semi-supervised classification with graph convolutional networks. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1609.02907                                    .")\]. Additionally, other architectures such as graph attention networks \[ [25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR25 "Velickovic P, Cucurull G, Casanova A, Romero A, Lio P, Bengio Y (2017) Graph attention networks. Statistics 1050(20):10-48550")\] and graph isomorphism networks \[ [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR26 "Xu K, Hu W, Leskovec J, Jegelka S. (2018) How powerful are graph neural networks?. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1810.00826                                    .")\] have expanded on these concepts with alternative message-passing mechanisms, demonstrating efficacy in node and graph classification tasks.

In recent years, MoleculeNet \[ [27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR27 "Wu Z, Ramsundar B, Feinberg EN, Gomes J, Geniesse C, Pappu AS, Pande V (2018) MoleculeNet: a benchmark for molecular machine learning. Chem Sci 9(2):513–530")\], a comprehensive benchmark for molecular machine learning, has gained significant attention, particularly in tasks related to quantum mechanics and physical chemistry \[ [28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR28 "Rasool A, Rahman JU, Iqbal Q (2024) Optimizing GNN architectures through nonlinear activation functions for potent molecular property prediction. Computation 12(11):212")\]. The benchmark provides a platform for evaluating various models, including graph-based neural networks, which have shown remarkable progress in predicting molecular properties such as lipophilicity, hydration energy, solubility, and quantum mechanical characteristics. Rollins et al. \[ [29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR29 "Rollins ZA, Cheng AC, Metwally E (2024) MolPROP: molecular property prediction with multimodal language and graph fusion. J Cheminformatics 16(1):56")\] introduced MolPROP, a multimodal approach integrating language and graph-based techniques to enhance property predictions in these domains. Zhang et al. \[ [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR30 "Zhang Q, Mao D, Tu Y, Wu YY (2024) A new fingerprint and graph hybrid neural network for predicting molecular properties. J Chem Inf Model 64(15):5853–5866")\] proposed a hybrid neural network combining molecular fingerprints and graph representations to improve prediction accuracy for these critical properties. Tang et al. \[ [31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR31 "Tang B, Kramer ST, Fang M, Qiu Y, Wu Z, Xu D (2020) A self-attention based message passing neural network for predicting molecular lipophilicity and aqueous solubility. J Cheminformatics 12:1–9")\] leveraged a self-attention-based message-passing neural network for predicting lipophilicity and solubility, while Lee et al. \[ [32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR32 "Lee S, Park H, Choi C, Kim W, Kim KK, Han YK, Son Y (2023) Multi-order graph attention network for water solubility prediction and interpretation. Sci Rep 13(1):957")\] developed a multi-order graph attention network to interpret and predict water solubility. Furthermore, Zhang \[ [33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR33 "Zhang Z. (2024) MSGNN: multi-scale graph neural network for molecular property prediction. In 2024 7th international conference on computer information science and application technology (CISAT). IEEE: New York. Pp. 919–922")\] introduced the Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (MSGNN), focusing on the accurate prediction of molecular properties within the quantum mechanical domain.

While much research in molecular property prediction focuses on developing advanced GNN models to enhance performance, the challenges of large memory requirements, high computational load, and slow inference speed have not been widely addressed. GNNs demand substantial resources to process complicated graph-structured data, making large-scale molecular datasets difficult to handle. This issue becomes even more crucial for resource-constrained devices including mobile and embedded systems, restricting GNN deployment in real-world applications such as material design and drug discovery. Moreover, finding the right balance between model complexity and efficiency still an open challenge, as diminishing computational demand often leads to a loss in predictive performance. Without addressing these limitations, the widespread adoption of GNNs in molecular sciences will remain restricted, preventing researchers from fully leveraging their potential.

In the literature, researchers have explored and developed various techniques to enhance the computational efficiency of GNNs, including layer sampling \[ [34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR34 "Hamilton W, Ying Z, Leskovec J (2017) Inductive representation learning on large graphs. Adv Neural Inf Process Syst.                    https://doi.org/10.8550/arXiv.1706.02216                                    "), [35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR35 "Chen J, Zhu J (2018) Stochastic training of graph convolutional networks. Mach Learn.                    https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1710.10568                                    "), [36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR36 "Chen J, Ma T, Xiao C. (2018). Fastgcn: fast learning with graph convolutional networks via importance sampling. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1801.10247                                    ")\], graph sampling \[ [37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR37 "Zeng H, Zhou H, Srivastava A, Kannan R, & Prasanna V. (2019). Graphsaint: graph sampling based inductive learning method. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1907.04931                                    .")\], quantization \[ [38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR38 "Jacob B, Kligys S, Chen B, Zhu M, Tang M, Howard A, Kalenichenko D. (2018) Quantization and training of neural networks for efficient integer-arithmetic-only inference. In Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. Pp. 2704–2713.")\], knowledge distillation \[ [39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR39 "Hinton G. (2015) Distilling the knowledge in a neural network. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1503.02531                                    ")\], tensor decomposition \[ [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR40 "Novikov A, Podoprikhin D, Osokin A, Vetrov DP (2015) Tensorizing neural networks. Adv Neural Inf Process Syst 28")\], and pruning \[ [41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR41 "Han S, Mao H, Dally WJ. (2015) Deep compression: compressing deep neural networks with pruning, trained quantization and huffman coding. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1510.00149                                    .")\]. These methods aim to reduce memory consumption and computational costs while maintaining predictive performance. Recently, MetaGIN \[ [42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR42 "Zhang X, Chen C, Wang X, Jiang H, Zhao W, Cui X (2025) MetaGIN: a lightweight framework for molecular property prediction. Front Comp Sci 19(5):195912")\], a lightweight deep learning framework designed specifically for small molecules, has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets. It leverages 2-hop and 3-hop edges to capture 3D molecular features such as bond angles and torsion angles, making it particularly effective for molecular property prediction. However, its reliance on accurate 3D molecular geometries poses a limitation, especially for large datasets. Generating 3D structures at scale can be computationally expensive, potentially offsetting its efficiency gains and limiting its applicability in large-scale molecular modeling tasks.

Within these approaches, quantization is a feasible way to reduce memory storage requirements and computational costs by representing model parameters in fewer bits. Using a lower number of bits definitely speeds up matrix multiplication, but the right balance must be maintained between model performance and efficiency. Quantization techniques are broadly employed to boost efficiency across various hardware platforms, including large-scale systems such as GPUs and CPUs, as well as resource-constrained devices like IoT and edge devices. Several studies have explored quantization for GNNs, using different datasets and GNN architectures. Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Tab1) provides an overview of these works.

**Table 1 Quantization studies on GNN models**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3/tables/1)

As highlighted in Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Tab1), no prior literature exist which specifically applies quantization techniques in physical chemistry and quantum mechanics domains. These areas present unique challenges, such as small datasets (e.g., FreeSolv) and complex, large datasets (e.g., QM9), requiring a quantization method that is both flexible and adaptable to these constraints. Among these techniques, DoReFa-Net stands out as a simple yet effective quantization framework that supports flexible bit-widths, ranging from FP16 to INT8 and further down to INT4 and INT1. It does not require any hyperparameter tuning or specialized techniques before implementation, unlike several existing quantization methods. For example: EXACT (RP + INT2) requires careful tuning of the \\(\\frac{D}{R}\\) ratio, a primary hyperparameter that directly impacts performance, which adds complexity to the implementation. EPQuant, while efficient, requires precise adjustments to parameters like batch size and assignment compression, which can be time-consuming and may demand domain-specific knowledge. VQ-GNN, though specifically designed for GNNs, depends heavily on the quality of approximation provided by Vector Quantization (VQ). Implementing effective VQ in GNNs requires additional techniques to preserve graph properties and model performance. In contrast, DoReFa-Net is a general-purpose quantization method which can be easily adapted to different neural network models, including GNNs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to explore quantization in the above-mentioned fields, and DoReFa-Net’s simplicity, efficiency, and low-bit quantization capabilities make it an ideal choice for this pioneering research.

This study designs a training procedure to preserve end-to-end model performance after quantization and compares the results with existing literature to demonstrate its effectiveness. Weights and activations of GNN models are quantized using the DoReFa-Net algorithm, with models trained on the ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipophilicity (Lipo), and QM9 datasets. The main focus is on the prediction error of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) using the DoReFa-Net algorithm, with predictive performance evaluated using metrics such as Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). To analyze the impact of quantization, different precision levels, including FP16, INT8, INT4, and INT2, are applied to model parameters. A comprehensive comparison between full-precision and quantized models is presented both graphically and theoretically. ## Methods

### Datasets

The datasets, including ESOL, FreeSolv, and Lipo are directly loaded from PyTorch Geometric's MoleculeNet. These datasets focus on tasks such as estimating the logarithmic water solubility (ESOL), the hydration free energy of small molecules in water (FreeSolv), and the octanol/water distribution coefficient (Lipophilicity). The datasets contain 1128, 642, and 4200 molecules, respectively. The molecular representations are provided in SMILES format, which does not include spatial information. Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Tab2) presents detailed attributes of the first molecule from each dataset.

**Table 2 SMILES notation, graph visualization, and target values of the first molecule in each dataset**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3/tables/2)

The QM9 dataset, directly loaded from PyTorch Geometric, includes 19 molecular properties as target variables. It contains 130,831 molecules, each with detailed spatial information. For this study, the focus is solely on predicting the dipole moment (μ), although the dataset also provides other regression targets. Additionally, a subset of 30,000 molecules is used to keep the runtime manageable, while still providing sufficient data to demonstrate initial results.

Each dataset is randomly split into three subsets: training, validation (for parameter selection), and testing (for model comparison), with proportions ranging from 80 to 10%.

### Graph neural network

In GNNs, nodes update their states by gathering information from neighboring nodes. Different GNN architectures employ distinct methods to aggregate and combine this information for updating node states. This study focuses on two GNN architectures: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) \[ [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR24 "Kipf TN, Welling, M. (2016) Semi-supervised classification with graph convolutional networks. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1609.02907                                    .")\] and Graph Isomorphism Networks (GIN) \[ [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR26 "Xu K, Hu W, Leskovec J, Jegelka S. (2018) How powerful are graph neural networks?. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1810.00826                                    .")\].

### DoReFa-Net

The DoReFa-Net algorithm \[ [58](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR58 "Zhou S, Wu Y, Ni Z, Zhou X, Wen H, Zou Y. (2016) Dorefa-net: training low bitwidth convolutional neural networks with low bitwidth gradients. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1606.06160                                    ")\], commonly used in CNN applications, has been minimally explored in the context of property prediction task. The DoReFa-Net algorithm quantizes weights, activations, and gradients by using \\(k\\)-bit representations. Since this study focuses on the impact of quantization during the inference stage, no quantization is applied during training. Therefore, PTQ is adopted for both weights and activations to enable efficient deployment while maintaining computational and memory efficiency.

Weight Quantization: In this approach, weight values are quantized using Eq. [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Equ5).

$${f}\_{\\omega }^{k}\\left({r}\_{i}\\right)=2{quantize}\_{k} \\left(\\frac{tanh({r}\_{i})}{2max(\|tanh({r}\_{i})\|)}+ \\frac{1}{2}\\right)-1$$

(5)


The tanh function is used to limit the value range of weights to \[− 1,1\] before quantizing to \\(k\\)-bit. By construction, \\(\\frac{tanh({r}\_{i})}{2max(\|tanh({r}\_{i})\|)}+ \\frac{1}{2}\\) is a number in \[0,1\], where the maximum is taken over all weights in that layer. \\({quantize}\_{k}\\) will then quantize this number to _k_-bit fixed-point ranging in \[0,1\]. To mitigate the significant quantization error caused by a large input data range, an affine transformation is applied to adjust the output of \\({f}\_{\\omega }^{k}\\left({r}\_{i}\\right)\\) to the original range \[− 1,1\].

Activation Quantization: The input activations \\(r\\) are then quantized into \\(k\\)-bit values as defined in Eq. [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Equ6).

$$f\_{\\alpha }^{k} \\left( r \\right)\\; = \\;quantize\_{k} \\left( r \\right)$$

(6)


Before applying quantization on activations, it is assumed that the output of the previous layer has passed through a bounded activation function, which ensures \\(r \\in \[\\text{0,1}\]\\).

Equation [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Equ7) explains how both weights and activations are quantized in this method.

$${quantize}\_{k}= \\frac{1}{{2}^{k}-1} round ({(2}^{k}-1){r}\_{i})$$

(7)


### Implementation

This study integrates DoReFa-Net algorithm with GNNs to create lightweight models for property prediction tasks while maintaining desirable performance. DoReFa-Net serves as a uniform quantization approach that downscales the precision levels of network parameters. The process starts by training the model with full precision before the weight quantization step described in Eq. [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Equ8) take place.

$$q\_{k} \\left( w \\right)\\; = \\;round\\left( {\\left( {2^{k} - 1} \\right)\\left( {\\frac{\\tanh \\left( w \\right)}{{2 + \\max \\left( {\\left\| {\\tanh \\left( {w\_{i} } \\right)} \\right\|} \\right)}} + \\frac{1}{2}} \\right)} \\right)$$

(8)


When this approach executes it transforms continuous weight values (\\(w)\\) into \\({2}^{k}\\) discrete levels. Since weights remain fixed after training, it can be stored in fewer bits, reducing storage costs. Such compression enables efficient deployment of the model on various devices including smartphones, IoT devices and microcontrollers.

To constrain the activations within the range \[0,1\] and then quantized them, following Eq. [9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Equ9) is employed.

$$q\_{k} \\left( a \\right)\\; = \\;round\\left( {\\left( {2^{k} - 1} \\right)\\left( {\\frac{a}{{2 + \\max \\left( {\\left\| {a\_{i} } \\right\|} \\right)}} + \\frac{1}{2}} \\right)} \\right)$$

(9)


Equation [9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Equ9) maps activations (\\(a\\)) into a discrete set of cardinalities \\({2}^{k}\\). The bulk of operations including matrix multiplications perform at fixed-point integer which accelerates computation and reduces power usage compared to floating-point calculations.

This efficiency is achieved by using a reduced number of bits, with the quantization bit-width typically chosen as a power of 2, such as 16-bit, 8-bit, 4-bit or 2-bit. However, the model’s performance tends to suffer when bit-width becomes excessively reduced. The significant problem requires striking the right balance between system efficiency along with model performance.

In this study, the effects of PTQ on the molecular networks are replicated using the quantization effect simulation scheme, enabling the evaluation of quantization's impact on model performance before deployment, with weights and activations quantized as outlined in Eqs. [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Equ10) and [11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Equ11), repectively.

$$f\_{\\omega }^{k} \\left( {r\_{i} } \\right)\\; = \\;\\max \\left( {\\left\| {\\tanh \\left( {r\_{i} } \\right)} \\right\|} \\right) \\times \\left( {2quantize\_{k} \\left( {\\frac{{\\tanh \\left( {r\_{i} } \\right)}}{{2\\max \\left( {\\left\| {\\tanh \\left( {r\_{i} } \\right)} \\right\|} \\right)}} + \\frac{1}{2}} \\right) - 1} \\right)$$

(10)


$$f\_{\\alpha }^{k} \\left( r \\right)\\; = \\;\\max \\left( {\\left\| {r\_{i} } \\right\|} \\right) \\times \\left( {2quantize\_{k} \\left( {\\frac{a}{{2\\max \\left( {\\left\| {a\_{i} } \\right\|} \\right)}} + \\frac{1}{2}} \\right) - 1} \\right)$$

(11)


In the end, rescaling by \\(max(\|tanh({r}\_{i})\|)\\) and \\(max(\|{r}\_{i}\|)\\) ensures that the quantized weights and activations maintain their original magnitude, preserving their relative importance after quantization.

## Experiments and results

### Experimental settings

To achieve optimal performance, each GNN model is obtained after extensive hyperparameter tuning across four datasets. The training loss is calculated using Mean Squared Error (MSE), defined as \\(\\frac{1}{n}\\sum\_{i=1}^{n}({{y}\_{i}-{y}\_{i}{\\prime}}^{2})\\). All experiments are conducted over 100 epochs with a learning rate of 0.001, using the Adam optimizer \[ [59](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#ref-CR59 "Kingma DP. (2014) Adam: A method for stochastic optimization. arXiv preprint                    arXiv:1412.6980                                    ")\]. The batch sizes are set to 16 for the ESOL, LIPO, and FreeSolv datasets, and 64 for the QM9 dataset.

The experiments take place within the Google Colaboratory environment, utilizing an NVIDIA T4 Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) for computational tasks. An Intel Xeon Central Processing Unit (CPU) and 12 GB RAM provide additional processing and support. Training and testing procedures are implemented using the PyTorch Framework. Both training and inference phases utilize the same hardware configuration.

### Limitations of current study

Although meaningful insights into the effects of quantization models on property prediction tasks have been provided, certain aspects remain underexplored due to time and resource constraints. These limitations are summarized to avoid over-generalizing the findings and to emphasize potential areas for future research.

- This work investigates the impact of PTQ on GNN models through simulation rather than real hardware implementation. The simulation of quantization does not account for hardware-specific effects, such as variations in precision handling across different devices.

- This work focuses on PTQ but does not consider quantization-aware training (QAT). Exploring both techniques could provide deeper insights into their respective impacts, especially in terms of model performance during training and inference.

- The paper investigates uniform precision levels (e.g., W16A16, W8A8) but does not explore mixed-precision strategies (e.g., W8A4, W2A16), which might yield better model performance.

- Quantization is applied to weights and activations, but not on the node features and adjacency matrix. Extending quantization to these matrices could provide a more complete understanding of how full model quantization affects both performance and efficiency.

- The study uses a subset of 30,000 molecules from the QM9 dataset and evaluates only the dipole moment property. This limits the generalizability of the findings to other molecular properties and tasks. Further research on a broader set of molecular properties and tasks could provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the quantization techniques.


## Conclusion

This study integrates the DoReFa-Net quantization algorithm with GNN models to address computational efficiency challenges in molecular property prediction tasks using MoleculeNet benchmark datasets, such as ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipo, and QM9. While previous research has mainly focused on model effectiveness, this work prioritizes computational efficiency without compromising performance. Various quantization levels, including 16-bit floating-point (FP16) and integer formats (8-bit, 4-bit, and 2-bit), are evaluated using RMSE and MAE. The results indicate that GNN models, especially those with GCN layers, achieve comparable or slightly improved performance up to 8-bit precision across all datasets, significantly reducing storage and computational demands. In contrast, GIN models exhibit reduced robustness to quantization, consistently showing suboptimal performance across all bit-widths, with the exception of the quantum mechanical dipole moment (μ) task. These findings highlight that selecting an appropriate GNN variant for quantization is crucial for physical chemistry datasets, as these datasets yield comparable performance for GCN models but show suboptimal performance for GIN models at INT8 precision. For the QM9 dataset, both models demonstrate comparable performance to the baseline up to INT8. However, since the discussion focuses on a single task, the results may vary for other tasks. Further investigation is needed to draw a definitive conclusion about whether the performance is influenced by the architecture, the task, or both. Additionally, DoReFa-Net's performance at extreme quantization levels, such as 4-bit and 2-bit, appears unsuitable for achieving optimal results. These limitations highlight the need for future research to develop more robust techniques or hybrid approaches to balance computational efficiency and performance.

### Appendix A: model architecture

The high-level descriptions of the GCN and GIN model for both types of datasets are presented in Tables [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Tab5) and [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Tab6). Variations in the architecture arise from datasets originating from different domains, each with distinct molecular structures and properties. While using the same model design for each domain-specific dataset may yield optimal results for one domain, it may not perform as well for others. Therefore, to achieve better model performance, optimal frameworks are designed to effectively capture the complexities of each dataset.

The models are implemented using PyTorch Geometric, with manual hyperparameter selection based on prior experience and existing research. This manual approach ensures reliable assessment conditions, reduces computational costs, and enhances reproducibility. The results indicate that manual tuning performs effectively in this work; however, further refinement through optimization techniques could enhance performance.

### Appendix B: model evaluation on a single batch

In Figs. [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Fig8), [9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Fig9), [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Fig10) and [11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-00989-3#Fig11), each point on the plot represents the predicted and truth outcomes for the target task of the molecules. If two points with different colors are close together, their estimated value is approximately similar to the actual value. Overlapping points indicate that the predictions and ground truth score matches. Points that are far apart suggest a large error between the estimated and target values. As seen in all baseline models, the model predictions and truth scores either overlap or are close to each other, indicating minimal error. However, in all INT2 models, the predicted and target points are farther apart, suggesting a higher error. In some cases, even when points overlap, it does not mean their estimated and actual values are the same; rather, it indicates that their indices are different, meaning they correspond to different molecules in the batch.

metadata.ogDescription: Efficient and reliable prediction of molecular properties, such as water solubility, hydration free energy, lipophilicity, and quantum mechanical properties, is essential for rational compound design in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have significantly advanced molecular property prediction tasks, their high memory footprint, computational demands, and inference latency are often overlooked. These challenges hinder the deployment of property prediction models on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT devices. Therefore, optimizing storage, reducing resource consumption, and improving inference speed are crucial. This paper presents a systematic approach to molecular networks by integrating GNN models with the DoReFa-Net quantization algorithm. The proposed method aims to enhance computational efficiency while maintaining predictive performance, enabling lightweight yet effective models suitable for molecular task. The study investigates the impact of different bitwidth quantization levels on model performance, using metrics such as RMSE and MAE. Results show that, for physical chemistry datasets, the effectiveness of quantization is highly dependent on the model architecture. Notably, the quantum mechanical dipole moment task maintains strong performance up to 8-bit precision, achieving similar or slightly better results. However, extreme quantization, particularly at 2-bit precision, severely degrades performance, highlighting the limitations of aggressive compression.

# Molecular Property Prediction Challenge

![](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/98094/images/header)

## Molecular Property Prediction Challenge

[Overview](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/molecular-property-prediction-challenge/overview) [Data](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/molecular-property-prediction-challenge/data) [Code](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/molecular-property-prediction-challenge/code) [Models](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/molecular-property-prediction-challenge/models) [Discussion](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/molecular-property-prediction-challenge/discussion) [Leaderboard](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/molecular-property-prediction-challenge/leaderboard) [Rules](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/molecular-property-prediction-challenge/rules)

## Overview

# Molecular Property Prediction Challenge

Welcome to the **Molecular Property Prediction Challenge** — a chemistry-meets-machine learning competition where your task is to build predictive models for **molecular dipole moments** using 3D molecular structures provided in XYZ format.

Molecular dipole moments are fundamental physical properties with applications in solvation, reactivity, spectroscopy, and material design. Accurate prediction of these values from structure alone is a key step in accelerating computational chemistry and materials science.

* * *

## Goal

Your objective is to **predict the dipole moment** of a set of small organic molecules, given only their 3D atomic structures.

This is **not** your typical clean tabular dataset — expect a **raw, scientific-format dataset** that will put your **data wrangling and preprocessing skills to the test**. You'll need to:

- Parse XYZ files for atomic symbols and 3D coordinates
- Extract relevant features (e.g., geometric, atomic, or descriptor-based)
- Decide how to represent molecules numerically (e.g., fingerprints, SOAP descriptors, graph-based embeddings)
- Clean, structure, and transform the data into a machine-learnable format

This competition is a **true test of your ability to handle real-world, messy scientific data** and turn it into insight. If you enjoy a challenge that mixes chemistry, machine learning, and engineering — this one’s for you.

* * *

## What You'll Learn

- Working with 3D molecular structure data (XYZ format)
- Extracting features using cheminformatics and materials informatics tools
- Dealing with missing or malformed data
- Training regression models for scientific properties
- Best practices in preprocessing pipelines and reproducibility

* * *

**P.S.** Don’t worry if you don’t have a background in chemistry — that’s part of the fun! You're encouraged to lean on tools like **ChatGPT**, **Perplexity**, **Claude**, or any other LLM of your choice to help you research, debug, and explore. The goal is to get you to use LLMs mindfully — you'll need to do research, write code, use esoteric python packages and ask the right questions to extract meaningful insights.

Start

Apr 4, 2025

Close

Apr 6, 2025

### Description

link

keyboard\_arrow\_up

## Description

This competition focuses on **predicting the dipole moment** of molecules from their 3D structural information. The data is provided in XYZ format (commonly used in computational chemistry), but you are **not expected to use the raw XYZ files directly** for model training.

Instead, your task is to generate **feature representations (descriptors)** that summarize molecular properties in a machine-learnable format.

* * *

## Descriptor Types

You are free to choose from a variety of descriptor types depending on your approach:

### 2D Descriptors

Computed from the molecular graph (bonds and connectivity), typically using the [SMILES string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Molecular_Input_Line_Entry_System) which needs to be obtained from the XYZ file coordinate data first.

Examples:

- Morgan fingerprints
- Molecular descriptors (e.g., molecular weight, hydrogen bond donors, etc.)

### 3D Descriptors

Computed from the 3D coordinates in the XYZ files.

Examples:

- SOAP (Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions)
- Coulomb matrices

Use libraries such as `RDKit`, `DScribe`, and `ASE` to compute these descriptors.

You may choose one or more descriptor types to build your regression model.

* * *

## Advanced Models

You are encouraged to explore **Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)** for this task. You may consider exploring available implementations of molecular graphs.

However:

> **Pretrained models are not allowed**. You must train your models from scratch and be able to explain how they work.

* * *

## Bonus Points for Descriptors

For each descriptor type you use (e.g., RDKit, Morgan, SOAP), you'll receive:

**+5 bonus points** if your model achieves a **Mean Square Error (MSE)** below 0.72 D, using a unique set of descriptors (eg. exclusively Molecular Descriptors or SOAP Descriptors, no combined descriptors)

Descriptor types must be clearly distinct to qualify for multiple bonuses.

* * *

## Leaderboard Points

Kaggle leaderboard positions contribute to your final score:

- 1st Place: 90 points
- 2nd Place: 80 points
- 3rd Place: 70 points
- 4th Place: 60 points

* * *

## Final Presentation Criteria

In addition to your leaderboard scores, the following criteria will be evaluated during your final presentation:

- **Presentation Clarity:** Your ability to clearly communicate your approach, methods, and insights.
- **Model Explainability:** How effectively you can explain your model's predictions, interpret feature importances, and justify modeling choices.
- **Innovation:** Creativity demonstrated in data preprocessing, feature engineering, model architecture, or overall approach.

Up to **15 additional points** may be awarded based on the clarity, depth, and originality of your insights.

Your deliverables may include a **presentation**, a **written report**, or a **Jupyter notebook**. **You must also share your code for evaluation.**

To be eligible to win and claim prizes, all participants **must be present** at the final presentation ceremony at **11:00 AM on Sunday, April 6**.

* * *

## ⚠️ Important Note for Participants Using Off-the-Shelf Neural Network Architectures

If your solution involves using **off-the-shelf neural network architectures** (such as Graph Neural Networks, SchNet, DimeNet, or similar advanced models), you are required to submit an additional document clearly explaining your chosen architecture and implementation details. Acceptable formats include:

- A **2-page written report**, or
- A **4-slide presentation**

This supplementary document will be collectively evaluated by the professors and stakeholders, scored out of **20 points**. Your final competition score will be penalized based on this evaluation:

- A perfect score ( **20/20**) results in **no penalty**.
- Any points lost from this evaluation will directly translate into a deduction from your final score (up to a maximum of **20 points**). For example, a score of **15/20** will result in a **5-point deduction** from your final competition score.

Ensure your supplementary document is clear, detailed, properly cites relevant resources, and demonstrates your understanding of the chosen model architecture.

* * *

## Getting Started Tips

- Do understand that you CANNOT work directly with xyz file data (atomic coordinates) unless you're using a GNN. And personally, I would advise everyone to NOT begin with GNNs. Begin with 2D descriptors.
- **For 2D descriptors, you first need to convert the xyz coordinate data into [SMILES strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Molecular_Input_Line_Entry_System).** Consider using the 'RDKit' library to obtain descriptors like Morgan Fingerprints and Molecular Descriptors.
- Use `DScribe` and `ASE` to extract 3D descriptors like SOAP.
- Use `scikit-learn`'s regression models like Ridge/Lasso Regression and Random Forest. Note that the descriptors can make the data very high dimensional, and this can lead to bad time scaling for some regressor models.
- Handle NaNs, missing files, and failed conversions gracefully.

* * *

This competition emphasizes not only model performance, but also data understanding and thoughtful preprocessing. Expect to spend a significant portion of time on cleaning and engineering your inputs. Good luck!

### Evaluation

link

keyboard\_arrow\_up

Submissions are evaluated using **Mean Squared Error (MSE)** between the predicted and actual dipole moments.

Lower MSE indicates better performance.

* * *

## Submission File

For each molecule ID in the test set, you must predict its **dipole moment**. Your submission should be a **CSV file** with exactly two columns:

- `ID`: The molecule identifier (e.g., `mol_1`, `mol_2`, etc.)
- `dipole_moment`: Your model’s predicted value (a floating-point number)

The file must include a header and follow the format below:

```apache
ID    dipole_moment
mol_1    3.353
mol_2    1.134349313
mol_3    2.181779306
mol_4    2.825665
content_copy
```

# Enhancing Molecular Property Prediction   with Knowledge from Large Language Models
## Introduction
In particular, the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in the molecular domain has shown significant promise, as molecules can naturally be represented as graph structures. These models can be trained end-to-end directly on molecular graphs, enabling them to capture higher-order nonlinear relationships more effectively, eliminate human biases, and dynamically adapt to different tasks (Wu et al.

In recent years, numerous GNN-based methods have been proposed, many of which focus on developing improved self-supervised learning techniques (Liu et al. [2021b](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib27)), leveraging contrastive learning (Khosla et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib20)), and deriving more robust molecular representations from large volumes of unlabeled molecular data (Liu et al. For example, by explicitly constraining chemical bonds between molecules and targets, Interformer (Lai et al. [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib22)) can predict more plausible chemical conformations. Similarly, the incorporation of multiple sequence alignments enables AlphaFold to more accurately predict molecular and protein conformations (Jumper et al. More relevantly, LLM4SD (Zheng et al. [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib52)) leverages LLMs to extract human knowledge for molecular vectorization, subsequently employing Random Forests for MPP, and outperforms GNN-based methods on several tasks.

In this work, we propose the integration of knowledge from LLMs with molecular structural information to enhance MPP. [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib12)).

## Related work
### Expert-crafted feature based MPP.
Molecular descriptors are quantitative features or attributes extracted from molecular structures. These features can range from simple numerical values to complex mathematical expressions and are used to describe the physicochemical properties, topological structures, and electronic characteristics of molecules (Khan et al. Molecular fingerprints, on the other hand, are binary vectors or bit strings used to represent molecular structures.

## Experiments
The BACE dataset focuses on human beta-secretase 1 inhibitors, providing both quantitative IC50 values and qualitative binary labels for small molecule inhibitors across a broad affinity range. It includes 154 inhibitors for affinity prediction, 20 for pose prediction, and 34 for free energy prediction.

These include GraphMVP (Liu et al. Given that deep neural networks are capable of capturing nonlinear relationships directly from complex data, we integrated all descriptors provided by LLMs, removed any thresholds, and directly used the raw descriptor features in combination with structural features.

## References

###### Abstract

Report issue for preceding element

Predicting molecular properties is a critical component of drug discovery. Recent advances in deep learning—particularly Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)—have enabled end-to-end learning from molecular structures, reducing reliance on manual feature engineering. However, while GNNs and self-supervised learning approaches have advanced molecular property prediction (MPP), the integration of human prior knowledge remains indispensable, as evidenced by recent methods that leverage large language models (LLMs) for knowledge extraction. Despite their strengths, LLMs are constrained by knowledge gaps and hallucinations, particularly for less-studied molecular properties. In this work, we propose a novel framework that, for the first time, integrates knowledge extracted from LLMs with structural features derived from pre-trained molecular models to enhance MPP. Our approach prompts LLMs to generate both domain-relevant knowledge and executable code for molecular vectorization, producing knowledge-based features that are subsequently fused with structural representations. We employ three state-of-the-art LLMs—GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and DeepSeek-R1—for knowledge extraction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our integrated method outperforms existing approaches, confirming that the combination of LLM-derived knowledge and structural information provides a robust and effective solution for MPP.

Report issue for preceding element

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1/figs/fr2.png)Figure 1: (a) Traditional machine learning algorithms rely heavily on expert knowledge and feature engineering, limiting their adaptability and generalization. (b) Graph neural networks, while directly mapping molecular graphs to properties, often ignore expert insights. (c) We bridges these gaps by using LLMs to incorporate expert knowledge with graph structures, enhancing the prediction of molecular properties.Report issue for preceding element

## Introduction

Report issue for preceding element

Predicting molecular properties is an essential task in the drug discovery process. Computational approaches to MPP not only accelerate drug screening but also improve cost efficiency. Traditional computational methods for molecular property prediction (MPP) typically involve extracting molecular fingerprints or carefully engineered features, followed by the application of machine learning algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVM) (Cortes and Vapnik [1995](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib6 "")) and Random Forests (RF) (Ho [1998](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib15 "")). However, these methods heavily depend on domain experts for feature extraction and are susceptible to human knowledge biases (Merkwirth and Lengauer [2005](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib32 ""); Degen et al. [2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib8 "")). The advent of deep learning has partially addressed these limitations. Deep learning approaches can better leverage the growing availability of data and are less reliant on manual feature engineering. In particular, the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in the molecular domain has shown significant promise, as molecules can naturally be represented as graph structures. These models can be trained end-to-end directly on molecular graphs, enabling them to capture higher-order nonlinear relationships more effectively, eliminate human biases, and dynamically adapt to different tasks (Wu et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib44 ""); Mayr et al. [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib31 ""); Wieder et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib43 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

In recent years, numerous GNN-based methods have been proposed, many of which focus on developing improved self-supervised learning techniques (Liu et al. [2021b](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib27 "")), leveraging contrastive learning (Khosla et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib20 "")), and deriving more robust molecular representations from large volumes of unlabeled molecular data (Liu et al. [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib26 ""); Wang et al. [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib41 "")). However, we contend that human prior knowledge will remain indispensable for the foreseeable future. For example, by explicitly constraining chemical bonds between molecules and targets, Interformer (Lai et al. [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib22 "")) can predict more plausible chemical conformations. Similarly, the incorporation of multiple sequence alignments enables AlphaFold to more accurately predict molecular and protein conformations (Jumper et al. [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib18 "")). More relevantly, LLM4SD (Zheng et al. [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib52 "")) leverages LLMs to extract human knowledge for molecular vectorization, subsequently employing Random Forests for MPP, and outperforms GNN-based methods on several tasks. LLMs such as ChatGPT (OpenAI [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib33 "")) and DeepSeek (Guo et al. [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib12 "")) have been trained on vast amounts of human data and are finely aligned with human knowledge through techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback (Bai et al. [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib1 "")), endowing them with a breadth and depth of knowledge that surpasses most individuals. Nevertheless, the molecular knowledge acquired by LLMs intuitively follows a long-tail distribution. For well-studied molecular properties, LLMs may have accumulated sufficient experience, but for less-explored areas, they may lack adequate reference rules. Furthermore, due to the well-known phenomenon of hallucination, LLMs often provide seemingly plausible answers even when they lack sufficient knowledge. While LLM4SD offers an effective means of utilizing the knowledge embedded in LLMs, it cannot fully eliminate hallucinations and biases. Therefore, we argue that integrating molecular structural information—particularly representations learned from pre-trained structural models—with human prior knowledge represents a highly promising direction for advancing MPP.

In this work, we propose the integration of knowledge from LLMs with molecular structural information to enhance MPP. Similar to LLM4SD, we extract prior knowledge from LLMs based on different types of molecular properties and further prompt LLMs to infer potential knowledge by providing molecular samples related to the target properties. We instruct the LLMs to generate both relevant knowledge and executable function code, which are then used to vectorize the molecules and obtain knowledge-based molecular features. These extracted knowledge features are subsequently fused with structural features obtained from pre-trained molecular structure models. By combining knowledge features with structural features, our model not only leverages the breadth of human expertise but also learns direct mappings between structure and properties from the structural features. We employ three state-of-the-art LLMs for knowledge extraction, including GPT-4o, GPT-4.1 (OpenAI [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib33 "")), and DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al. [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib12 "")). Extensive comparative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and confirm that LLMs can provide reliable knowledge for MPP.

### Expert-crafted feature based MPP.

Report issue for preceding element

Many earlier MPP models were based on expert-crafted features, primarily including two categories: molecular descriptors and molecular fingerprints. Molecular descriptors are quantitative features or attributes extracted from molecular structures. These features can range from simple numerical values to complex mathematical expressions and are used to describe the physicochemical properties, topological structures, and electronic characteristics of molecules (Khan et al. [2016](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib19 "")). Molecular fingerprints, on the other hand, are binary vectors or bit strings used to represent molecular structures. They map molecular structures to a fixed-length bit string, where each bit typically indicates the presence or absence of a specific substructure or chemical feature (Barnard and Downs [1997](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib2 ""); Sheridan et al. [1996](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib38 ""); Danishuddin and Khan [2016](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib7 "")). The performance of such models often depends on the selection and quality of these expert features (Zhang et al. [2017a](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib49 ""); Fan et al. [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib10 "")). These expert-crafted features are commonly used to train traditional machine learning models, such as LightGBM, random forest, and support vector machines (Zhang et al. [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib50 ""), [2017b](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib51 "")). Additionally, some studies have used molecular fingerprints as input features to train more modern deep neural network architectures, such as BERT (Wen et al. [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib42 "")) and GNN (Cai et al. [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib5 "")).

### Graph-based MPP

Report issue for preceding element

Molecules can naturally be viewed as graph structures, where atoms are considered as nodes and covalent bonds between atoms as edges. With the advancement of graph neural networks (GNNs), many studies have shifted towards using GNNs for MPP tasks. However, training deep neural networks requires a substantial amount of high-quality labeled data. Due to the scarcity of labeled molecular data, previous work has explored various methods to enhance model prediction capabilities, such as pre-training, contrastive learning, and knowledge augmentation. Pre-training involves constructing self-supervised learning tasks and training on large unlabeled datasets to obtain better initial weights, thereby improving the model’s predictive performance on downstream tasks. Common self-supervised paradigms include node attribute reconstruction, context learning, and constructing multi-view graphs for contrastive learning (Veličković et al. [2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib40 ""); You et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib48 ""); Xia et al. [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib46 "")). Contrastive learning methods enhance model generalization by aligning different modalities of molecules through contrastive loss, and can also be considered a form of pre-training task (Liu et al. [2021a](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib25 ""); Kuang, Ren, and Ren [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib21 ""); You et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib48 ""); Xiang et al. [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib47 ""); Wang et al. [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib41 "")). Knowledge augmentation aims to improve the model’s understanding of molecules by leveraging external knowledge bases. For instance, KPGT (Li et al. [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib24 "")) utilizes additional knowledge as molecular labels, enabling the model to effectively capture both structural and semantic information within molecular graphs.

### LLM-based MPP

Report issue for preceding element

With the significant success of LLMs in general domains, recent efforts have been made to leverage language models (LM) or LLMs for MPP. For instance, (Liu et al. [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib29 "")) replaced the CHEML IDs of molecules in the training corpus with SMILES sequences to create text data encapsulating SMILES, and then fine-tuned MolT5 (Edwards et al. [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib9 "")) to predict molecular properties and translate between molecules and natural language. Similarly, (Liu et al. [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib28 "")) developed a mixed instruction set based on SMILES to fine-tune LLaMA, achieving notable performance in few-shot and zero-shot MPP. MolFM (Luo et al. [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib30 "")) trained a multimodal foundational model for molecules by integrating knowledge graphs, molecular structures, and natural language. BioT5 (Pei et al. [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib34 "")) jointly trained on SELFIES of molecules, protein sequences, and natural language, also enabling MPP and related tasks.

Report issue for preceding element

However, these approaches require extensive fine-tuning of the language models to learn the mapping between molecules and natural language from large datasets, rather than directly extracting human knowledge about molecules from pre-trained LMs. Existing general LLMs, such as ChatGPTs (OpenAI [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib33 "")) and DeepSeeks (Guo et al. [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib12 "")), have been thoroughly trained on vast human knowledge bases, suggesting they may have internalized human knowledge and experience regarding molecules. LLM4Mol (Qian et al. [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib35 "")) annotates molecular sequences using ChatGPT and employs the embeddings of the annotated text for downstream tasks. LLM4SD (Zheng et al. [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib52 "")) extracts task-related rules using LLMs, vectorizes molecules based on these rules, and then trains a random forest model for MPP. Both methods utilize the knowledge LLMs have acquired from human experience but overlook the structural information inherent in molecules.

Report issue for preceding element

Intuitively, the molecular knowledge learned by LLMs from human corpora follows a long-tail distribution. For well-researched molecular properties, LLMs may have acquired sufficient experience, whereas for knowledge lacking extensive research literature, LLMs might not provide adequate reference rules. Therefore, incorporating the intrinsic structure of molecules is essential for molecular-related tasks. This work proposes the first method for MPP that combines LLM-driven knowledge with molecular structure.

We leverage the knowledge provided by LLMs as molecular knowledge features. Drawing inspiration from LLM4SD, we extract both prior knowledge and inference knowledge. Prior knowledge refers to information that LLMs have acquired from extensive human literature, while inference knowledge is derived from the LLMs’ reasoning capabilities, enabling them to infer knowledge from a limited number of samples. LLM4SD implements knowledge extraction in a segmented manner: it first assigns the LLM the role of a chemistry expert to summarize a set of judgment rules based on the task type or to infer possible rules from given molecular samples. These rules are then passed to another code LLM, which generates executable code accordingly. We optimize this process by designing prompts that instruct the LLM to directly generate both the rules and the corresponding executable function code. ## Experiments

Report issue for preceding element

Datasets. The HIV dataset, derived from the Drug Therapeutics Program AIDS Antiviral Screen, contains results from testing over 40,000 compounds for their ability to inhibit HIV replication, with outcomes categorized as confirmed inactive, active, or moderately active. The BACE dataset focuses on human beta-secretase 1 inhibitors, providing both quantitative IC50 values and qualitative binary labels for small molecule inhibitors across a broad affinity range. It includes 154 inhibitors for affinity prediction, 20 for pose prediction, and 34 for free energy prediction. The ClinTox dataset contrasts FDA-approved drugs with those that failed clinical trials due to toxicity, featuring classification tasks for 1,491 compounds based on clinical trial toxicity and FDA approval status. The BBBP dataset, originating from a study on blood-brain barrier permeability, offers binary labels indicating whether compounds can penetrate the BBB. This dataset supports the development of machine learning models for predicting BBB permeability, which is crucial for drug discovery and the design of neurological therapeutics (Wu et al. [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib45 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

Baselines. Since our goal is to enhance the capabilities of pre-trained molecular structure models through knowledge integration, we selected several classic pre-training models as baselines and backbones. These include GraphMVP (Liu et al. [2021a](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib25 "")), GraphCL (You et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib48 "")), InfoGraph (Sun et al. [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib39 "")), AttrMask (Hu et al. [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib16 "")), ContextPred (Hu et al. [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib16 "")), EdgePred (Hamilton, Ying, and Leskovec [2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib13 "")), GPT-GNN (Hu et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib17 "")), and GROVER (Rong et al. [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib36 "")). All comparative experiments were conducted using the same molecular scaffold dataset split, with model parameters set to the default values provided by the respective authors. Furthermore, we observed that the extracted knowledge primarily relies on the Descriptors modules of RDKit (Landrum [2013](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib23 "")) for molecular descriptor extraction. Given that deep neural networks are capable of capturing nonlinear relationships directly from complex data, we integrated all descriptors provided by LLMs, removed any thresholds, and directly used the raw descriptor features in combination with structural features. This approach was designed to assess whether LLMs possess inherent feature selection capabilities. We refer to this control group as GNN+Desc, and its model architecture and training parameters are identical to those of the experimental groups.

Report issue for preceding element

Metrics. Many studies on MPP evaluate models solely using the Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC AUC) ( [Fang et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib11 ""); Liu et al. [2021a](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib25 ""); Wang et al. [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib41 "")). This metric considers recall and false positive rates across various thresholds, providing a comprehensive assessment of model performance. However, in highly imbalanced datasets, ROC AUC can yield overly optimistic evaluations. For example, in the ClinTox dataset, the ratio of positive to negative samples is 1:12.19, rendering ROC AUC insufficient as a sole metric. Therefore, in addition to ROC AUC, we also employ precision as an evaluation metric. Precision measures the proportion of true positive samples among those predicted as positive, offering more meaningful insights in scenarios with imbalanced class distributions.

Report issue for preceding element

Knowledge Extraction. We extract both prior knowledge and inference knowledge for each task from three mainstream LLMs: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and DeepSeek-R1. The prompts used for this process are detailed in Appendix 1. For inference knowledge that requires sample data, we randomly select 50 positive samples from each training set, using the same samples across all LLMs to ensure consistency.

Report issue for preceding element

### Experimental result

Report issue for preceding element

The overall experimental data are presented in Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#Sx3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Method ‣ Enhancing Molecular Property Prediction with Knowledge from Large Language Models"). For a more intuitive comparison, these data are also visualized in Figures 7, 8, 9, and 10 in Appendix. Based on the experimental results, we can draw the following conclusions:

Report issue for preceding element

Integrating knowledge extracted from LLMs can effectively enhance the performance of MPP. Although different pre-training strategies may lead models to different local optima, incorporating knowledge from LLMs almost always results in performance improvements. Taking the knowledge provided by GPT-4.1 as an example, the most significant improvement was observed on the ClinTox dataset, where the ROC AUC increased by up to 9.41%, and an average increase of 2.91%. On the HIV, BACE, and BBBP datasets, improvements were also observed, with average increases of 4.54%, 2.37%, and 1.58%, respectively. We also observed that, under certain pre-training strategies, integrating knowledge could occasionally lead to negative gains. For example, on the BBBP dataset, the AM method experienced a 0.11% decrease in ROC AUC after the integration of knowledge from DeepSeek-R1.

Report issue for preceding element

The knowledge provided by different LLMs has varying impacts on model performance. Overall, GPT-4.1 achieved the highest average improvement across all four datasets, with increases of 4.54%, 2.37%, 2.91%, and 1.58%, respectively. On the HIV, ClinTox, and BBBP datasets, DeepSeek-R1 provided a greater average improvement than GPT-4o, whereas on the BACE dataset, GPT-4o yielded a larger gain.

Report issue for preceding element

Directly integrating all molecular descriptors does not necessarily lead to improved performance. Although the direct fusion of all descriptors resulted in an average increase of 0.96% on the BACE dataset in ROC AUC, it actually led to a decrease in ROC AUC performance on the ClinTox and BBBP datasets. Specifically, on the ClinTox dataset, the GNN+Desc. approach resulted in an average 1.76% decrease in ROC AUC, which is 13.88%, 15.93%, and 14.84% lower than the results achieved by GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and DeepSeek-R1, respectively. On the BBBP datasets, GNN+Desc. also exhibited average decreases of 1.76% compared to the baseline models. These results demonstrate that leveraging prior knowledge provided by LLMs is indeed more effective than simply combining all descriptors in a brute-force manner. We also observed that, on the HIV dataset, incorporating all descriptors led to features that were excessively sparse and highly similar, causing the model to suffer from vanishing gradients and fail to generate accurate predictions. We will analyze these features in detail in the next section.

Report issue for preceding element

### Knowledge Analysis

Report issue for preceding element

Knowledge visualization. In addition, we visualized the knowledge extracted from different LLMs. Figure [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#Sx3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Method ‣ Enhancing Molecular Property Prediction with Knowledge from Large Language Models") presents the visualization results of knowledge features from different LLMs on each dataset. In each subfigure, each row represents a molecule, and each column represents a feature dimension. The first 100 rows correspond to 100 randomly selected positive samples, while the last 100 rows correspond to 100 randomly selected negative samples. We can observe that for the HIV, ClinTox, and BBBP datasets, the knowledge provided by each LLM exhibit clear and visually discernible discriminative power between positive and negative samples. However, for the BACE dataset, these knowledge vectors do not display any obvious visual discriminative ability. Therefore, in such cases, it is essential to incorporate molecular structural information.

Report issue for preceding element

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1/figs/vz_desc.png)Figure 4: Visualization of vectors using all molecular descriptors. From left to right, the datasets are HIV, BACE, ClinTox, and BBBP.Report issue for preceding element![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1/figs/spearman_prior.png)Figure 5: Prior Knowledge and the Spearman Rank Correlation Coefficient of Molecular Properties.Report issue for preceding element

For comparison, we also visualized all descriptor features on the four datasets using the same settings. As shown in Figure [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#Sx4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Knowledge Analysis ‣ Experiments ‣ Enhancing Molecular Property Prediction with Knowledge from Large Language Models"), the results for HIV, BACE, ClinTox, and BBBP are displayed from left to right. It can be observed that, for ClinTox and BBBP, these descriptors also exhibit some visually discernible differences between positive and negative samples, but the differences are less pronounced than those in the knowledge vectors. Moreover, the descriptor vectors are much longer than the knowledge vectors provided by the LLMs, making it more challenging for the model to directly learn specific patterns from all the descriptors.

Report issue for preceding element

Correlation between knowledge and molecular properties. We separately analyzed the correlations between prior knowledge and inference knowledge generated by LLMs and molecular properties, using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (Sedgwick [2014](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#bib.bib37 "")). For prior knowledge, we compared the correlations between LLM-generated prior knowledge and molecular properties with those between all descriptors and molecular properties. As shown in Figure [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.20664v1#Sx4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Knowledge Analysis ‣ Experiments ‣ Enhancing Molecular Property Prediction with Knowledge from Large Language Models"), the correlations for prior knowledge vary considerably across different datasets. On the BBBP dataset, prior knowledge generated by all three LLMs shows a high correlation with molecular properties, outperforming native descriptors. On the BACE dataset, the correlation of prior knowledge is also satisfactory. However, on the HIV and ClinTox datasets, the overall correlation between LLM-generated prior knowledge and molecular properties is significantly lower than that of the native descriptors.

Report issue for preceding element

For inference knowledge, as shown in Figure 6 in Appendix, the correlation with molecular properties is higher on the BBBP and ClinTox datasets compared to HIV and BACE. Notably, on BBBP and ClinTox, some inference knowledge achieves a correlation greater than 0.5, indicating a strong association. Overall, the inference knowledge generated by GPT-4o demonstrates a relatively high correlation.

Report issue for preceding element

Knowledge redundancy and conflict. When extracting prior and inferential knowledge, we explicitly require each LLM to provide at least 10 rules. For example, in the ClinTox task, our prompts for extracting prior and inferential knowledge are as follows: “How can one determine if a molecule has clinical toxicity based on its SMILES? Please provide at least 10 computational rules for assessment and a Python-based computational method. Each rule should be implemented as a function that takes a molecule as input and returns a 0/1 value.” and “How can one determine if a molecule is toxic based on its SMILES representation? Please infer possible criteria from the clinically validated toxic SMILES provided below, and offer at least 10 computational methods using Python. Each rule should be implemented as a function, with the input being a molecule and the output being a 0/1 value. Below are the molecules that have been clinically validated as toxic:……”

Report issue for preceding element

| HIV | 2/20 | 6/20 | 0/20 | 2/20 | 1/20 | 3/20 |
